newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ortega warns of property war in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Ortega warns of property war in Nicaragua.

text.p: Former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega on Monday said Nicaragua was nearing "total war" over the ownership of thousands of disputed properties and called on legislators to order a stop to a wave of evictions.

"The war over property has started here. Blood has started to flow. If the government and its legislators in the National Assembly do not vote in favour of the law that suspends these evictions it will be a declaration of total war," Ortega told a news conference.

Ortega said the death of two people in recent weeks in violent court-ordered evictions was just a small taste of things to come if Nicaragua's National Assembly does not approve a Sandinista-sponsored law halting these evictions.

Ortega said that since the Sandinistas and the right-wing government of President Arnoldo Aleman began talks to resolve the property problem on Jan. 27, there has been a wave of court-ordered evictions of families who received confiscated land during the 1979-1990 leftist Sandinista government.
He said the passage of the law to temporarily halt these evictions until the talks resolve the issue was a basic condition for a renewal of the talks, which were suspended indefinitely on Feb. 27.
He did not say when the law would be voted on by the National Assembly.

Speaking live on Nicaraguan state radio from Barcelona, Spain, where he was attending an Inter-American Development Bank meeting, Aleman tried to calm nerves after Ortega's comments saying poor people would not be kicked off their land.
"As we have said before, we are going to give legal security to the thousands and thousands of poor people who have their lots of land," he said.
Aleman said his Liberal Alliance party would also present its own property bill in the National Assembly, but did not specify the date or bill's content.
At issue were more than 200,000 private houses, farms and businesses confiscated by the Sandinistas, many of which are being reclaimed by their former owners.

The previous government of President Violeta Chamorro, which left office on Jan. 10, tried and failed to resolve the property problem, which continued to threaten Nicaragua's political stability and scare away investors.
